title: Hunter Valley Sémillon
subtitle: A dry wine that ages like magic

steps.title: Picked early
steps.body: The Hunter Valley, north of Sydney, is hot and humid, with rain often at harvest. Growers pick Sémillon early, at around 10 to 11% alcohol, before the rain and rot. The wines are fermented in steel, without oak or malolactic, and bottled early. Young, they're lean, lemony and grassy, with high acidity.

steps.title: The transformation
steps.body: With 5 to 10 years in bottle, often under screw cap, Hunter Sémillon transforms: it develops toast, honey, lanolin, lemon curd and nutty notes, as if it had been oaked. It isn't: these flavours come from bottle ageing. The best can age 20 years or more.

steps.prompt: Hunter Valley Sémillon's toasty notes come from oak ageing.
steps.explanation: Not true. It's usually unoaked; toast and honey develop with bottle age.

steps.body: If you find a 10-year-old Hunter Valley Sémillon, open it next to a young one. The difference shows how far bottle ageing can take a simple, unoaked wine.

steps.prompt: Why is Hunter Sémillon picked so early?
options: To avoid harvest rain and rot, and keep acidity
steps.explanation: Early picking keeps freshness and avoids the region's harvest rains.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Hunter Sémillon is picked early, at 10 to 11%, unoaked
With age it gains toast and honey, without oak
